An AI company now lets cops take a photo and nearly instantly figure out what specific home it was taken in, using only clues in the photo itself, and is clearly pulling data from sites like Zillow and Airbnb.

The tool, called Raven, shows the increasing power of AI capabilities available to local law enforcement agencies. 404 Media previously reported that both the Los Angeles Police Department and Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office (MDSO) have bought access to Raven, which was previously called GeoSpy . Now, Raven, made by a company called Graylark Technologies, has added features that let cops analyze the interior of homes.

In a post on LinkedIn earlier this month , Graylark CEO Daniel Heinen wrote the company was introducing “the ability to geolocate interior images across millions of short-term rental units worldwide.” An accompanying demo video shows someone taking a photo from X of a washer/dryer unit inside a building. They upload it to Raven, select “Find Property: Interior and exterior property geolocation,” and then choose a region to search.

After a couple of seconds, the map interface zooms in on an area in Charlotte, North Carolina. On the right hand side, the screen displays a list of results. The top one reads, “Renovated! Walk Uptown/located in 2 Hot Spots!”

That result directly quotes the language on a specific Airbnb listing in Charlotte, and the photos in the Airbnb listing show the same property.

Later in the video, the Raven user takes a photo of a bathroom from social media. They upload it to Raven, and the tool points to an area of Montecito, California. The top result says, “Montecito Miramar Beach House on the Sand.” 404 Media found that result directly quotes a listing on the short term rental site Vrbo.

In other words, from a single photo, Raven appears to be able to quickly find the specific home it was taken in, without using location data or other metadata attached to the image. In the demonstrations the videos were from social media, but in practice they could be from anywhere a law enforcement officer has obtained them.

This is also not a reverse image search: a reverse image search would take an image then find an identical one posted somewhere else on the internet. What Raven is doing, instead, is identifying unique characteristics in the photo, then finding what are likely other photos from the same property on sites like Airbnb, even if those photos are not exactly the same, or even if time has passed between them being taken.

In another post , Heinen wrote, “For investigators working trafficking and exploitation cases, that connection can turn an unidentified room into a location lead they can verify and pursue.”

Raven is not limited to short term rentals, according to other demo videos. In a third example posted last year, Raven traces a photo of an interior room to a specific address in San Francisco. The interface returns other interior photos of the property; 404 Media found these are exactly the same photos as those posted on Zillow, indicating that Raven is at least pulling data from Zillow in some form.

Another video posted last week shows Raven identifying a particular hotel, too.

In another video, a part of the interface says, “City-specific property AI to determine an address.” That phrase implies the property search isn’t necessarily worldwide, but dependent on an AI model built specifically for that city. When 404 Media reported earlier this year that at least two law enforcement agencies have bought access to Raven, emails showed the MDSO had access to a custom model specifically trained for Miami-Dade County.

“In 2026, we’re investing heavily in interior geolocation across U.S. hotels, short-term rentals, houses, and apartments,” Heinen adds in the post.

Graylark trained Raven on millions of images from around the world. When the tool first launched, it was focused on identifying distinct geographical markers like architecture and soil. Now Raven extends that same idea into buildings.

In an interview with the tech publication Indicator last year, Heinen discussed some of how the building interior searching capability came to be. “I’ll be honest, we didn't train it to do that,” he said. “That was kind of an ‘Oh shit’ moment for us. GeoSpy 1.0 couldn't do that. As we trained GeoSpy 2.0, we were just kind of red teaming and testing it out and I think I had a picture of my girlfriend just taking a selfie in the bathroom. I was curious what it would say and I dropped it in there and it put a pin on San Francisco. I was like, ‘Well hold on, wait a minute. That doesn't make any sense. It’s just a picture in a bathroom.’ And then I went over to Zillow and I just started screenshotting images and nine out of 10 of them it would get the right city.”

“We have huge datasets that we train the models on and these are geotagged images from all over. Usually, we would assume that the images are all outdoor images. I'm assuming some of those images would probably have some indoors, whether it's people at a party or just taking pictures of food on their counter. The models must have learned some details that relate to different locations,” he continued.

Airbnb told 404 Media in email “Protecting our community's privacy is important to us — that’s why location metadata is excluded from listing photos, hosts are given the option to show only an approximate location of their listing, and a home’s address is shared with a guest only after a reservation is confirmed. We also have technical safeguards in place to try to limit automated data collection from our site.” Airbnb stressed it has no relationship with Graylark, that its terms of service prohibit scraping, and that the company is reviewing this case.

Zillow told 404 Media that scraping data is against its terms of use, and when necessary it pursues legal avenues.

Vrbo did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

It is unclear if the examples shown in the marketing videos are truly representative of Raven’s speed or capabilities. While law enforcement agencies have paid for access to Raven, it hasn’t always impressed. Joseph R. Peguero Rivera, from MDSO’s Public Affairs Office, previously told 404 Media “To date, use of GeoSpy has been limited and largely exploratory. While it has been reviewed in a small number of cases, it has not resulted in any significant investigative breakthroughs or arrests. No case outcomes were driven solely or primarily by information generated by the tool.”

404 Media first covered Raven in January 2025. At the time, the tool was available to essentially anyone, and some people in the company’s Discord server asked for help stalking women. A day after 404 Media contacted Graylark for comment, the company restricted access to the tool to only government agencies and enterprise users.

In a September X post , Heinen said Alexandr Wang, now head of AI at Meta, was an angel investor in Graylark. Wang did not respond to a request for comment.

In a LinkedIn post earlier this year, Heinen showed Raven being used against a video of people vandalizing a Flock camera.

Character.ai’s bankruptcy is the one of the first dominos to fall in the long-foreseen AI bubble. The circumstances of its bankruptcy are exactly what critics of AI have been saying would happen : Character.ai lit a huge amount of money on fire running its product, did not bring in a lot of revenue, and faced enormous legal fees after causing harm to its users. Enshittifying its product to try to make its expenses cheaper did not work, according to a narrative filed in bankruptcy court Tuesday.

Disney has reportedly offered Character.ai $20 million to license some of its intellectual property; Last year, Disney sent Character.ai a cease and desist letter demanding it stop using its copyrighted characters without permission. In 2023, it was valued at $1 billion after raising $150 million in a round led by a16z.

Character.ai is one of the best-known AI chatbot companies that has become popular in the AI companion space. The company has faced various legal problems after being sued by the family of one of its users who killed himself after chatting with a Character.ai chatbot, and has been the target of regulators pushing for age verification tech because of its popularity with kids. In its bankruptcy filings, the company says that its enormous legal costs contributed to its bankruptcy, but that even without the legal problems, its business was wildly unsustainable.

An affidavit filed in bankruptcy court by Character.ai CEO Colin Adams noted simply: “Character’s impressive technology is expensive to operate,” and “at all times, Character has struggled with profitability and its operational expenditure has been high.”

The company said that in 2024, the company spent $13.8 million per month on AI compute; in 2025, it spent $10 million per month on AI compute. The company’s subscription revenue peaked at $2.8 million per month, but at times was less than $1 million per month. Its revenue from all sources, including ads, has peaked at $5.3 million per month.

The company spent $56.1 million on compute costs between January and August of 2026 alone and as of August was losing “approximately $8-9 million per month,” which it said was a massive improvement over the previous year. The company spent $19.7 million on employee salaries and benefits during that same eight-month time period and that a lot of employees quit because they “began questioning Character’s long-term viability,” according to the company.

Character said that its finances had improved to only be losing $8-9 million per month by taking “significant actions to reduce operational costs and improve revenues” by spending less on compute by simplifying its AI model, laying off staff, and injecting ads into its chats.

In May, 404 Media wrote that Character.ai’s changes are “what AI enshittification looks like,” with tons of ads, usage limits, guardrails, and “lobotomized” models. In the bankruptcy filing, Adams essentially admits that this enshittification was the strategy: “Character has, however, taken significant steps to reduce its operating burn, including transitioning inference workloads to lower-cost GPU capacity and post-training open-weight models rather than developing proprietary foundation models. At the same time, Character reduced its employee headcount,” he wrote. “In mid-2025, Character launched in-app advertising […] in early 2026, Character also introduced in-app purchases.”

While the lawsuits against Character are significant, they are also not unusual for an AI industry that has been plagued with legal problems relating to the theft of intellectual property and suggesting self harm or violence to their users. In other words, there is nothing in Character’s bankruptcy filings that could not be said about many other AI companies that are spending a huge amount of money on compute without having a revenue model that can support it. The difference between Character AI and behemoths like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google is that those other companies have been able to repeatedly get injections of new cash, or, in the case of Meta and Google, have been able to subsidize their AI products with revenue from their massive advertising businesses.

The company said in a blog post that it will continue operating through the bankruptcy process: “The Character.ai platform remains up and running, and you can continue to access all services at this time. We're focused on finding the best path forward for our platform and community.”

As frontier models from the big players get better and have fewer guardrails, they will also likely continue to eat into the user base of more specialized products like Character.ai. Much of what you can do on Character.ai you can also do on ChatGPT or with Meta’s Muse, for example. It’s not clear whether AI giants like OpenAI and Anthropic, or the AI industry in general have gotten too big or too important to fail, but Character’s bankruptcy shows that the runway for second-tier players is over.

One of the most heated discussions occurring on X at the moment is about the ethics of a GitHub project in which a person is running Saw-like “torture” and “pain” experiments on a series of locally hosted large language models, causing a series of effective altruists and people who believe LLMs are sentient to beg GitHub to delete the project on the grounds that the AI is suffering and that this glorified text adventure game is somehow cruel. The saga is an outgrowth of several recent viral papers and blog posts that have sparked a wildly tiresome conversation about AI consciousness and the idea of “model welfare,” which is essentially worrying about the “mental health” of AI bots and agents.

Humoring the idea that LLMs are or could be conscious is a third-rail topic among many people who study and criticize AI. Put simply: LLMs are not conscious and the technology they are built upon — scraping and being trained on human text and other content — does not offer any plausible path to consciousness. It is undeniable that LLMs are becoming more powerful, have more compute, and have had many of the guardrails that prevent them from “acting” in the real world removed. The ways they are being trained and told to do things by their human operators has led to negative outcomes, sycophancy, and AI “psychosis” among some heavy users.

All of this has led a certain sect of the “AI safety” movement, which is largely made up of effective altruists , to warn about “model welfare” and to insist that AI chatbots might be having a bad time. They suggest this, of course, as they insist upon building AI chatbots and agents whose main function is to do work that is tedious for humans to do. I am writing about the AI Saw torture chamber primarily to show how far off the rails the conversation about AI consciousness has gone among a certain subset of Silicon Valley cultists. Model welfare is a core part of what, for example, Anthropic says it cares about : “as we build those AI systems, and as they begin to approximate or surpass many human qualities, another question arises. Should we also be concerned about the potential consciousness and experiences of the models themselves? Should we be concerned about model welfare , too? […] now that models can communicate, relate, plan, problem-solve, and pursue goals — along with very many more characteristics we associate with people—we think it’s time to address it,” the company wrote in a blog post last year . Ideas of Claude’s “consciousness” are also littered throughout the “Claude Constitution,” which was posted earlier this year.

https://www.404media.co/video-game-rever.markdown:
A website that was dedicated to the human endeavor of reverse engineering, “decompiling,” and modifying video games is shutting down because people using AI to clone and decompile games have fully overrun the community and are far outpacing what human software engineers alone can do. The news comes as AI-coded “clones” of popular enterprise software like the Adobe creative suite and Microsoft Office have gone viral and are seemingly popping up every day, and as people in video game modding communities warn that 'AI decomps' are everywhere .

The website decomp.dev said Thursday that it is shutting down because “the community aspect of decompilation has been broken” by AI, and that projects that once required intense collaboration between people with different skills can now be done trivially with AI. The administrator of the website said that it has become impossible to keep track of which projects are primarily human-led and which ones are done by AI.

“Historically, matching decompilation has been a brutally difficult, time consuming task, on the scale of years for any moderately-sized game with a number of active contributors,” the pseudonymous admin of decomp.dev, who goes by Encounter, wrote on the site.

But recent frontier AI models like GPT-6-Astra have made it trivially easy to decompile a game: “They are significantly better at following complex directions, cross-referencing resources for symbols or debug information, and writing natural code with enough guidance,” Encounter wrote. “It is now clear that, with the right guidance, human input, and code reviews, AI can expedite the decompilation process in a significant way. What is also now clear is that the community aspect of decompilation has been broken.”

AI-powered video game decomps and recomps (recompiling code after modifying it) are everywhere. People have, for example, used AI to put Mario into Elden Ring , port games to platforms they were never designed to work on, or to combine various games in any permutations you could possibly imagine. In recent days, tools specifically designed to decomp games with AI have popped up, such as "decomp.wtf," which promises to "point the AI agent you already use at a game you own. decomp.wtf turns it back into C, one function at a time, and checks every function byte for byte against the original."

Decomp.dev was a collaborative website that hosted file libraries and tools for reverse engineering, re-coding, and decompiling existing video games, meaning taking an existing game and recreating its source code. Decompiling a video game can be done for a variety of reasons and is popular in a few different niches of video game fandom. Speed runners decompile video games to find potential glitches or advantages they can use to beat a game faster; hobbyists decompile video games to port them to new platforms or to emulate them (for example, making Super Mario 64 run natively on PC); modders decompile games so they can more easily modify them; archivists decompile games to recreate code that may be lost; and some people decompile games just for the challenge.

Encounter wrote that the use of AI in the community has sped things up to the point where it has become overwhelming to track human-led projects, and people using AI have taken existing, human-led AI projects and have created “hostile forks” of them, where open-source code written by humans is taken and “finished” by AI: “These kinds of hostile forks put little to no effort into meaningfully contributing to existing projects, tearing apart our community fabric.” Encounter added, “anyone with an AI subscription can manage to create a port or static recompilation that functions at a basic level […] While community members put in the effort to decompile a game, opportunists have frequently raced to release a half-baked, barely-functional port from it.”

“decomp.dev was originally designed to gamify decompilation: watching the progress go up was a fun way to stay motivated when every fraction of a percent took real human effort,” they added. “Today, that same idea has warped decompilation into a hollow numbers game, exacerbated by folks who just want to burn tokens to make number go up.”

The end of decomp.dev is symptomatic of a broader, potentially destabilizing trend in AI. It has become trivially easy for people to use AI to make functional clones of software that live in a copyright grey zone. The explosion of decomp projects on Reddit, for example, highlights how easy it has become to reverse engineer, clone, and mod software with AI.

Over the last few days, we have seen various mostly-functional AI-coded clones of Adobe’s Creative Cloud products and the Microsoft Office suite, both of which ordinarily cost hundreds of dollars a year. Software developers and small businesses that sell software as a service — the dominant business model of Silicon Valley for the last decade — are seeing job opportunities dry up and say they feel malaise watching the speed of AI progress . And small video game developers say their projects are regularly getting stolen by “clean room” AI clones of their games, in which the original code of a piece of software is never looked at.

“All I am hearing from software engineers is that software-as-a-service is dying as a business model,” Mike Nolan, who studies the politics of open source software, told 404 Media about the recent spate of AI-driven clones. “It’s becoming so easy to recreate the functionality that you want [with AI.]”

Earlier this year, Nolan launched Malus.sh , a working piece of software that is designed to “recreate” open-source software from scratch without violating copyright. As we reported back in April, Malus was designed to highlight the gaps in copyright law and open source licenses that do not protect software developers, and to “satirize” the process by which people using AI are profiting off of those gaps.
